content: The study aimed to gather extensive details across various thematic areas. However, responses to certain questions, particularly those concerning the content of transition and adherence counseling, were insufficiently detailed, limiting the ability to evaluate the quality and comprehensiveness of the counseling provided. Additionally, not all survey respondents answered every question, and the large sample size made individual follow-up to address gaps impractical. To mitigate this limitation, the text includes boxes summarizing survey type, sample size, and response rates for specific items (e.g., HL, n=125, rr=85%). The findings are not representative of all countries included in the research, as the analysis was restricted to facilities within the PATA network and other similar networks, rather than a random sample of facilities. Notably, non-PATA facilities were primarily sourced from the West and Central African sub-regions, which exhibit significant heterogeneity in health facilities. For example, the average number of adolescents in care at clinics was 367, with a standard deviation of 827, and the distribution of facilities across urban (50%), peri-urban (17%), and rural (33%) settings suggests a reasonable level of diversity. Although coders underwent training on coding rules before data analysis, inter-rater reliability was not calculated. Furthermore, due to time constraints, survey responses in Portuguese and French were back-translated into English using automated web-based translation tools. While this process may have compromised some nuances, prior comparisons of translations have demonstrated sufficient accuracy to justify its use. Lastly, the data relied on self-reporting by healthcare staff, and further validation of results through on-site assessments or engagement with other stakeholders (including adolescents) was not feasible due to the scope of the research and sample size. Ethical considerations were addressed by informing participants, both prior to and during the consent process, that they could withdraw from the study at any time without penalty or loss of benefits. For web-based surveys, ethical consent was obtained before respondents accessed the survey items. For email and fax submissions, respondents were required to send a signed consent form along with their responses. In the 218 facilities sampled across 23 countries, healthcare providers identified several prominent challenges in providing treatment and care to HIV-infected adolescents. The most frequently cited challenge, reported by 40% of respondents, was non-adherence and treatment resistance. Socioeconomic barriers, such as poverty, transportation costs, and food insecurity, were reported by 25% of respondents, followed by resource limitations and lack of privacy or space in facilities (24%). Other challenges included stigma, myths, and reliance on traditional medicine; adolescent behavioral issues, drug fatigue, and denial; poor caregiver support or orphanhood; loss to follow-up; and staff shortages, attrition, attitudes, or knowledge gaps. Less frequently reported challenges included unavailable drug formulations, stockouts, lack of adolescent-friendly services or materials, difficulties addressing sexual and reproductive health (SRH) needs, patient mobility, medication side effects, pill burden, boarding school environments, school scheduling conflicts, mental health issues, transition-related challenges, opportunistic and co-infections, delayed presentation, and substance abuse. Approximately 26% of surveyed facilities reported not having an official working definition of adolescence. This was particularly notable in West and Central Africa, where 49% of facilities lacked such a definition. Definitions of childhood, adolescence, and adulthood varied widely, with the start of adolescence reported to range from 8 to 21 years. While 57% of facilities defined adolescence as beginning at 10 years of age, only 13% defined adulthood as starting at 20 years. Regarding data monitoring, 66% of facilities maintained records that distinguished adolescents from other patient populations. However, 18% made no distinction between children, adolescents, and adults, while 11% recorded adolescents as children, and 4% recorded them as adults. Facilities in West and Central Africa reported the lowest rates of adolescent identification in records (53%). Treatment outcomes data were monitored by most facilities, with 77% tracking loss to follow-up rates, 75% monitoring first-line treatment regimens, 72% tracking second-line regimens, and 17% monitoring third-line regimens. However, only 20% of facilities disaggregated treatment outcomes by age. East African facilities reported better monitoring of treatment outcomes compared to their West, Central, and Southern African counterparts, except for third-line regimens, which were best monitored in Southern Africa. Notably, 42% of facilities in West and Central Africa reported not monitoring any treatment outcomes. The most common clinical presentations among HIV-infected adolescents included delayed growth and puberty (89%), skin conditions (84%), and opportunistic infections (82%). Other presentations included chronic lung disease (48%), mental health issues (41%), neurocognitive impairment (21%), lipodystrophy (9%), and malnutrition (7%). Adherence challenges were a significant issue, with 84% of facilities reporting ongoing difficulties. Other challenges included defining treatment failure in the absence of viral load monitoring (48%), lack of second-line treatment options (27%), and lack of appropriate drug formulations (20%). Less common challenges included side effects (9%), pill burden (7%), poor caregiver support or orphanhood (5%), staff knowledge and skills (2%), and laboratory issues (2%). Efforts to improve adolescent adherence included peer support groups, home visits, adherence counseling, and general counseling. Peer support activities were considered the most effective, followed by adherence counseling and community health worker engagement. However, the effectiveness of these interventions was largely based on anecdotal evidence, with limited targeted research conducted. Adherence counseling was offered at 87% of facilities, with the highest rates in East Africa (97%) and the lowest in West and Central Africa (69%). Counseling sessions often involved counselors, doctors, nurses, and caregivers, with less frequent involvement of community health workers, pharmacists, psychologists, social workers, and peer supporters. Many facilities lacked guidelines for managing adolescents with adherence challenges. Where guidelines existed, they recommended adherence counseling, caregiver engagement, peer support, and home visits. Viral load monitoring was available at 60% of facilities, with routine testing conducted every six months or annually in most cases. However, some facilities only performed viral load testing when treatment failure was suspected. In cases of confirmed viral load failure, common interventions included adherence counseling (65%), switching to second-line ART regimens (65%), staff consultations (35%), and repeating viral load tests (33%). Other interventions included caregiver engagement, opportunistic infection screening, and health education.
